notes: The thaw has set a clock on the house: the road carries a cart by noon, and the Major means the housekeeper's account heard and the papers signed before it. Four small stands are asked of you: at the grate, at your own barred door, over the sherry glass in your drawer, and to the doctor's question; the ewer carries you past the tallow stub, and the main stair carries you down to the drawing room.
opening: The eaves have begun to drip, and the lodge-keeper has waded up to say the road will carry a cart by noon. Major Carrington has ordered the carriage, barred you from the first floor, and sent Lavinia Netherby up to the study grate with pails, a fresh scuttle and the ash sieve; Mr Ellingham has gone up after her and called the maids down in law's name, and from the gallery rail his voice and the Major's cross above your head. Wet coal drips from the hod on the landing; Lavinia has not come down, and the Major's step is on the main stair behind you.

variants.text: The hall chair is set square across your door, and the key is on your side of the lock. Fairbrother has left it there and is looking at the half-landing window as if he had not.
The hall chair is set square across your door. The key has been turned from his side, and he holds it in the hand that is not holding the candle.
At the foot of the stairs Lavinia has your candle ready, unlit, held out in red hands before you ask for it.
At the foot of the stairs Lavinia stands with your candle unlit and looks from the Major's door to the lawyer's to the valet's chair; she waits for Fairbrother's nod before she lifts it.
Grey snow light through the half-landing window. Wet coal drips from the hod set down on the stair-rods, the sieve beside it, and the barometer has begun, for the first time in three days, to rise.
Breakfast was laid here, the dining room being cold; Mrs Ormsby's cup stands by the doctor's, and she praised the housekeeping to him across you, loudly enough for the Major.
Breakfast was laid here, the dining room being cold. Mrs Ormsby took her tea in her room and sent the tray down untouched; it stands on the library table still.
The deed box is open on the library table, the inkstand filled, the wax jack lit. The papers lie squared for signing, and the master's reading chair has been turned to the wall.

The Major's door stands open so that the gallery may be watched from inside it. Mr Ellingham waits on the Turkey runner with his hat in his hand, as a man waits who has said a thing in law's name and means to be seen having said it.

Pails stand along the Turkey runner where the maids set them down and left. Mr Ellingham waits by the case of waxwings; the widow's door is shut, and the snow light through the gallery windows has gone the colour of dishwater.
The study door is shut again and the bare boards swept. Whatever was in the grate is in the grate no longer, or in an apron, or down the back stairs.
The study door stands open for the first time since the night. Lavinia kneels at the dead grate with the sieve, the fire bucket beside her, and grey ash sifts through a trembling mesh.

options.detail: down the back way; rake the grate yourself
options.label: send her down; rake the grate yourself
options.text: You put her out by the back way and kneel to the grate yourself. Under the ash is a curl of paper that was not coal, and it is in your apron, or very nearly, when the step reaches the door: either the Major finds the grate raked clean and you on your feet, or Ellingham finds you kneeling with your hands black and has you out of the study in law's name.

options.detail: at the grate; go down to the lawyer
options.label: leave her at the grate; go to Ellingham
options.text: You leave her the sieve and go down to Mr Ellingham. Behind you the Major comes in and finds the girl alone at the grate with ash on her apron, and she does not know whose order to give him.

options.label: 'She found nothing, sir.'
options.text: You stand in the door and say it. The Major looks past you at the girl, and the girl goes down the stair with her apron held shut in both hands.

options.label: 'Steady the sieve. Breathe.'
options.text: She breathes. The sieve steadies a little, and the ash goes on falling through it, and the step goes on coming up the stair.

options.label: set a cup of tea by his chair
options.text: You open the door, set the cup on the boards beside his chair, and go back in. He drinks it. An hour later he says, to the wall and not to the door, that the master was warm at eleven.

options.detail: 'The heir will keep the house, Mr Fairbrother, and will ask who sat guard for the Major.'
options.label: 'The heir will ask who sat guard.'
options.text: He sets the cup down untouched. Forty years, he says, has outlasted heirs before, and he does not look at you when he says it.

options.detail: behind the linen press, to the gallery
options.label: slip through the linen press passage
options.text: The passage is black and smells of lavender and cold plaster. Either the press gives and you are on the study end in grey light with your eye to the keyhole, or it is locked from the gallery side and you come back to find Fairbrother has turned his chair to face the linen press and not your door.

options.label: 'Is the candle enough?'
options.text: 'It is wax, Mrs. It is enough.' He does not move the chair.

options.detail: in the ewer; back among the dozen
options.label: wash it; back among the dozen
options.text: The colour comes off the rim in the cold water and goes grey in the ewer. When the Major's man comes to turn the room over it is one of twelve on the tray, and you have nothing to say of ten o'clock.

options.detail: to Miss Gresham: what is in your drawer, and whose room is to be searched
options.label: send Lavinia to Miss Gresham
options.text: Lavinia goes up with the message and comes down without one. Millicent Gresham comes down herself a quarter-hour after, white to the lips, and asks you at the door what you want for it.

options.label: leave it under the account book
options.text: You lay the book over it again and shut the drawer. The water stands in the ewer and Lavinia goes on down the stair.

options.detail: 'Under the back stairs, sir. I did not look at the size.'
options.label: 'Under the back stairs; I didn't look.'
options.text: He nods, which is his habit, and says the widow has asked after the housekeeping, and goes to his own door.

options.detail: 'Outside Mrs Ormsby's door, sir. The hairpin lay under the keyhole.'
options.label: 'Outside Mrs Ormsby's door, sir.'
options.text: He says nothing, which is also his habit. The snow runs off his boots onto the flags, and he goes along the gallery to her door instead of his own.

options.label: 'You will want dry boots, Doctor.'
options.text: 'I will,' he says, and does not go to fetch them, and does not take his eyes off your face.

actions.label: carry the ewer down the maids' stair
actions.text: Going down with the ewer you pass Lavinia's door ajar. In her tin candlestick is a yellow tallow stub burned flat to the socket. The maids burn tallow; the study burns wax. A tallow stub among the study's wax would mean nothing of the maids, and everything of who carried a maid's candle upstairs.

actions.label: down to the drawing room, to give account
actions.text: You go down the main stair with your hands folded, past the wet hod and the sieve, to where the house is assembling to hear what the housekeeper saw.

events.text: Mr Ellingham comes down from the gallery and, passing you on the stair, names his price without lowering his voice: the unsigned will never passes your lips. The Major sets Fairbrother on the hall chair square across your door, takes Dr Ashcombe by the elbow, and walks him across the slush to the ice house himself.

Wheels in the slush below: the carriage is brought round. The Major's voice carries up the well of the stair: the house will assemble in the drawing room to hear the housekeeper's account of the night, and then the papers will be signed.

nudges.text: The Major's voice, from somewhere below: 'Noon, Ellingham. The road carries a cart at noon, and I will have her account before it.'
The drip from the eaves has found the coal hod and rings on wet coal, slow as a clock.

props.name: the ash sieve
props.description: A kitchen sieve, mesh gone grey. It shakes in Lavinia's hands, and a fine ash falls through it onto the bare boards.

props.name: the coal hod
props.description: Set down on the stair-rods where the maids dropped it when the lawyer called them down. Thaw water has got into it and drips wet coal onto the carpet.

props.name: the sherry glass
props.description: In your drawer, under the account book: the glass from the study at ten o'clock, a crescent of Miss Gresham's lip colour on the rim.

props.name: the ewer
props.description: Your own ewer, full of water drawn before the Major barred the stair. The water is very cold.

props.name: a cup of tea
props.description: Brewed on your own spirit lamp behind the door; the only tea in the house this morning not poured by a maid.

props.name: the servants' passage
props.description: A papered door at the back of your room, opening on a black passage that comes out behind the linen press on the study end. Fairbrother lit the Major along it two nights since. He has not mentioned it.

props.name: the hall chair
props.description: Set square across your door, with a wax candle on the boards beside it. It is the chair from the hall; someone carried it up.

frame.composition: Low eye-level shot from the stair head, looking up the well of the main stair to the gallery rail and along to the open study door at the far end

Cornelius Ellingham on the gallery with his hat held against his chest, looking down
Lucius Carrington's shadow rising up the stair wall, one hand on the newel post
Reginald Fairbrother standing beside a hall chair with an unlit wax candle
